title: He washes their feet (John 13:1–17)
hookLine: the teacher kneels with a towel and washes twelve pairs of dusty feet

cards: The bathroom nobody cleans. The leaking trash bag. The diaper at three in the morning.
Every house has jobs that wait for someone else. Tonight, a room in Jerusalem, before the feast of the Passover. Roads were dust and dirt, and sandals don't keep much out.

In the Bible, washing feet is servant's work; in the book of Samuel, Abigail offers to do it as a handmaid. John mentions no servant here. He says that during supper, their teacher stands up from the table.

teach.h: HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.
teach.b: John opens with a line about love, in the King James Bible: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end."
Then Jesus gets up from supper, lays aside his outer clothes, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant.
"After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded."
One pair of feet after another, including the feet of Judas, who's about to betray him.
Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me."
And Peter, all or nothing as always, swings the other way: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." Afterward Jesus dresses, sits down, and asks: do you know what I've done to you?
You call me master and lord, and you're right. "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." I've given you an example.
Later that night he gives them a new commandment: love one another, as I have loved you.
In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and the name Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, is said to come from it.

teach.h: YE ALSO OUGHT TO WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.
teach.b: On that day some churches still wash feet, and popes have knelt with a basin too. Among the Brethren, some Mennonites and others, foot washing is part of the communion service.
The one who ends up with a crown of thorns starts the night with a towel.

how: On Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, many Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches wash feet during the service. Some traditions, including many Brethren and Mennonite churches, practice foot washing regularly with communion.

s: Jesus skipped Judas when he washed their feet
the text gives no exception. he washed the disciples' feet, and Judas was there.
Maundy comes from the Latin for commandment
mandatum, from the new commandment: love one another.
foot washing was a servant's job
in the Bible it's servant's work: Abigail offers to do it as a handmaid.

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher kneels in front of you with a basin and a towel to wash your feet. what do you say?
o: you shall never wash my feet.
games.why: Peter refuses: thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus says, if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me, and Peter asks for his hands and head too.

practice: Think of one humble task waiting for you, the dishes someone else left, the bin nobody takes out, the coffee pot, the shared bathroom, the email thread nobody wants to answer, and choose one to do without a word: no announcement, no hint, no post.
If you pray, you can offer it quietly.

wordCard.voice: Towel. The linen cloth the teacher tied around his own waist, dressed like a servant, before he knelt to wash each disciple's feet, even Judas's.

orig.note: Greek: a linen towel, borrowed from the Latin linteum. The cloth Jesus tied around his waist.

carryVoice: Your line: the towel is the crown. A teacher, kneeling with a basin. That's day sixty-four.
